text:
Which collection would you learn A to Z?

Over your lifetime as a pianist, which collection would you want to learn in its entirety? Would you even consider doing this in the first place?

For example, quite a few people learn the whole Chopin Etudes, or Beethoven sonatas. Has anyone on here done this? I'm not talking about learning only this one work in one go and nothing else, but learning it over a couple of years and keeping it as something to study over and over.

I'll go first. Collections I'm interested in (in order):

* Chopin Etudes
* Bach WTC
* Liszt Transcendental Etudes
* Debussy Preludes
* Beethoven sonatas

I'm quite drawn to Chopin Etudes for some reason. I think I just like figuring out the different techniques, and some are among my favourite Chopin pieces from a pure musical perspective (25/12, 25/5, 25/1, 10/9).

I'm reading through the whole WTC bit by bit. I've finished reading through book 1, and now I'm using it for warming up for my evening practice. I tend to spend some time on specific preludes and sometimes fugues, so I'll probably learn them all eventually. Plus is fascinating.

Liszt TEs are probably my second pick after Chopin's. The problem is how hard they are. I'm not entirely sure I'll ever be able to even get the hardest ones up to 80% or 90% polish, most likely not. And I'm not a big fan of all of them (no. 1 huh). But there's something about this work that's got a legendary aura and some of these etudes are peak music (no. 11 is my favourite).

Debussy Preludes are also very very interesting to me. There's so much variety in them, and they aren't as hard technically as other collections. I'll probably read through all of them as well and maybe work on about at least half of them over time.

The last one is... tricky. So many people love all Beethoven sonatas, but I don't really see the appeal. Some of them are among my favourite pieces of all times, but some others are quite meh (I dropped Op. 10 no. 3 this year, I just didn't enjoy the first movement to put in the work). I might read through all of them slowly, but I doubt I'll ever try to properly learn them all.

There are so many other good choices. Mozart or Haydn sonatas, Scarlatti sonatas (I'm also reading through all of them, one a day, I'm at K179), Scriabin sonatas (this would be really hard plus I don't like no. 4 and no. 1), etc.

**My personal pick would be Chopin Etudes**. I think I could spend a lifetime on this and not get bored. I'd pick Liszt TEs second if it wasn't for its difficulty, so I suppose I'd pick the WTC (also difficult but in a different way).

What's yours? Is there any book or collection you love and have fully learnt or are planning to? Ideally around 1h or longer (aka. not something short like Brahms op. 117).

I'm secretly hoping that someone will say "all Czerny etudes" :D
label: experience

text:
Help with Saint-Saëns PC2 opening cadenza?

Hello, 

I'm starting to work on the opening of Saint-Saëns 2nd concerto and I would love some outside ("pro") opinion on the fingering of a specific pattern. 

I have no problem with the initial upward movement. Both hand finally land a diminished 5th appart (A - Eb) and start a parallel scale downward: still no issue. My problem is with the broken diminished seventh arpeggios, zigzagging all the way down the keyboard a sixth appart.

The isolated pattern goes:

RH:  Eb-F# C-Eb   A-C   F#-A Eb...

LH:  F#-A   Eb-F# C-Eb A-C   F#...

For the right hand, my fingering for the above is 23 14 15 34, and I'm pretty quite happy with that. I didn't have to look for it, it literally jumped at me.

The left hand is where I was a doubt. If I play left-hand alone, the "right" fingering for me is 32 41 32 51. It's very fluid that way.

BUT, when I bring hands together, the left hand always goes to 32 41 32 ***41*** 32 41 32 ***41***. The 5 gets replaced by a 4. It works too, but I know/feel the other one, with the 5, is more efficient, more elegant, more relaxed for my hand. I think the 4 gets in there because on the right hand we have "34", and the 4 fingers on each hand must be somehow connected. Especially since the whole pattern also has 2 mirror occurences (23 againts 32, 14 against 41)

So, that's not a terrible issue. I think 32 41 32 41 can work at tempo. But it grates on me, I have a feeling the other one (32 41 32 51) is intrinsically better and the very fact that the right hand makes good use of 51 to reposition makes me think the left hand ought to do so as well. And I'm afraid this "hidden connection" between mirrored fingers is a false friend and will come to bite me later on.

I've been working on this for 30" and I'm at a point where I can do both at a slow pace but I still need to focus to stick in the 5. What do you think? Should I let go and let it be with 4 (I'm ready to bring the tempo up), or should I persist on slow practive until the 5 soaks in?

Thanks for reading, and sorry for the long and very specific rant :)

Questions I have about hours / practice in piano

Some people say that the best pianists practice for more than 10 hours every day, while others argue that practicing for just 2–4 hours with deep focus is sufficient.

Who is right? I’ve encountered both perspectives, but they generally boil down to two main ideas:

\- "You need to put in as many hours as possible to reach a high level of proficiency".

\- "You should practice for fewer hours to ensure the practice is effective; adding more hours won’t necessarily lead to improvement—and might even be counterproductive".

I’d love to hear your thoughts: how many hours do you think one should practice?

Also, a follow-up question: do you think one should practice every single day?

Some people recommend taking one day off per week—meaning without touching the piano—to let your hands rest and keep your mind fresh. Others insist on practicing every day (perhaps taking a vacation or an occasional rest day every few months). Still others suggest practicing daily, but with varying levels of intensity.

Would you recommend taking one day off from the piano each week, or should one practice every single day?

TL;DR

1. How many hours should be played in piano for best improvement? Not many like 1-2, or in the middle like 3-6 range, o even like +10? (of course thinking in terms of you having that much time)

Which composers wrote for piano the best?

Not necessarily your favorite composer for the piano, I mean in terms of how well-suited the techniques are for pianists. I personally think Chopin is the most ergonomic, and also Bach, Rachmaninoff, Liszt, Mendelssohn, Debussy, Mozart.

On the other hand, there are a lot of composers who did not write very well for the piano despite being brilliant composers with amazing and famous works. Like Schumann, Brahms, Ravel, and a lot of late Beethoven.

1918 Ellington Upright Piano for $250 - First Piano

I got my first piano about 10 days ago for FREE off of Facebook Marketplace. I've been using an old keyboard, and always wanted a piano. This started three weeks ago at my local thrift store. I saw a huge pedal organ, Victorian, wood carving, it was gorgeous. I thought about getting it, but I still wanted a piano as it's more useful than an organ in the long run. So.. I found this one on Facebook. It's a circa 1918 Ellington made by Baldwin. The owner was moving, and if nobody reached out, it was going to the dump. Just in time, 5 days before, I inquired so we got it checked out and the only cost was $250 to move it to my house. It's not tuned yet, but the tuner/mover says it's not far off. Good shape, just dirty and well used. I wonder what stories it's got, if it was in a home, or a church, or a saloon or something. Don't have much information but it was incredibly cheap and I'm happy to have my own piano.
